Okay, speak. Odile, they con— oh. Thank you very much. I'm a lawyer but an aspiring judge, so I took advantage of this. It's probably my only opportunity to sit as a judge on something. Under-Secretary-General, thank you very much for being present in this UNCSO dialogue. I'm Vasu Gounden, the Executive Director of ACORD, but it's my pleasure to represent the CSO core group in this session. Let me recognize Ambassador— 7 weeks in the US, in New York, So I can't say welcome, I'm not a New Yorker, but I'm sure the Under-Secretary-General can welcome you, she's a citizen of the country. And my sister Yebeka from our sister organization CMI. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this session on the UN CSO Dialogue. We gather, as we said, at a remarkable time. In history. For more than 3 decades, many of us have lived and worked through an era defined by hope. The end of the Cold War unleashed powerful aspirations for a rules-based international order, democratic governance, human rights, inclusive development, and peaceful cooperation among nations. Peacebuilding emerged as one of the defining projects of that era, and we've had the privilege of working with the peacebuilding architecture for the last 20 years as a court. Around the world, civil society organizations, community-based organizations, faith-based leaders, women, youth movement, and the local peacebuilders became indispensable actors in shaping our societies. Technology amplified their voices, information flowed more freely, citizens organized, mobilized, and influenced public policy on a scale previously unimaginable. For a time, it appeared that history was moving in one direction, that humanity, despite setbacks and contradictions, was steadily advancing towards a more peaceful, more inclusive, and more democratic world. But history, as we know, rarely moves in a straight line. Today, Excellencies and colleagues, the foundations of that era are under strain. We are witnessing the return of great power competition. Multilateralism is increasingly challenged. National interest often trumps collective interest. Military expenditure is rising while development and peacebuilding resources are shrinking. Political polarization is deepening. Social cohesion is fraying. Trust in institutions is declining. At the same time, another profound transformation is underway. The concentration of economic, technological and information power in the hands of a relatively small number of actors is reshaping the nature of influence itself. The race for artificial general intelligence, quantum computing, advanced biotechnology and data dominance is creating centres of power whose reach increasingly transcends national borders. We are witnessing the emergence of actors whose influence rivals and in some cases exceeds that of many states. And so we must ask ourselves a difficult question: Who will shape the future of peace? Will it be governments alone? Will it be markets? Will it be technological elites? Or will it remain a shared human project shaped by governments, citizens, communities, institutions, all working together? These are not abstract questions, ladies and gentlemen. They go to the heart of peacebuilding, because peacebuilding has never simply been about ending violence. Peacebuilding is about determining who belongs, who participates, who benefits and who has a voice in shaping the future. Many of us in this room have devoted our entire lives to this work. I see my friend Gus here. Gus and I are like dinosaurs in this field. Jurassic dinosaurs. We have sat across negotiating tables in moments when war seemed inevitable and watched adversaries choose dialogue instead. We have worked in refugee camps, villages, cities and capitals. We have seen societies shattered by violence, and we have seen them rebuilt through courage, compromise and hope. We know from experience that peace is possible. But we also know that progress is not permanent. Every generation inherits the responsibility to defend and renew the institutions, values and relationships that make peace possible. No generation receives that inheritance guaranteed. The danger before us is not only conflict. The danger is our resignation, the belief that the forces shaping our future are now so large, so powerful and so technologically advanced —that ordinary people no longer matter, the belief that communities no longer matter, the belief that civil society no longer matters, the belief that peacebuilders no longer matter. History tells us otherwise. History reminds us that every great advance in human dignity began with people who were told they were too small to make a difference. The abolition of slavery, the expansion of democracy, the advancement of women's rights— look at all of our colleagues who would not have been here 100 years ago in the same room— the defeat of apartheid in my own country, South Africa— we didn't think that was possible— the protection of human rights. None of these achievements were inevitable. All of them were won because ordinary people refused to accept that the future belonged only to the powerful. And yet, colleagues, Excellencies, we must also be honest about the challenge before us. There is a real risk that what once appeared to be a democratic transition begins to resemble an autocratic permanence. A world in which power becomes increasingly concentrated, a world where stability is pursued without freedom, a world where efficiency replaces participation, a world where order replaces inclusion, a world where decisions affecting billions are made by a shrinking number of actors, a world that may become secure but not free. And perhaps beyond that lies another possibility: a technocratic future in which humanity gradually surrenders urgency and agency to the very systems it creates. A future in which machines become increasingly capable of making decisions once reserved for human beings. This future, Excellencies and colleagues, is one that may not be decades away. It may only be years away. This is why thinking about peacebuilding today requires us to think about tomorrow. We are no longer in 1990. We are no longer living in a moment defined by the collapse of a superpower and the expansion of a rules-based, values-driven order. We are living through a moment— in which power, technology, capital and geopolitics are converging in ways that could fundamentally reshape human society. This is the challenge of our time. And this is why peacebuilding must also evolve. We cannot simply recreate the models of the past. The world has changed. The actors have changed. The technologies have changed. The conflicts have changed. Therefore, peacebuilding must become more innovative, more inclusive, more anticipatory, more courageous. It must engage not only governments and civil society, but also technology companies, private capital, cities, faith communities, youth movements, and the next generation of global leaders. It must learn to operate in a world shaped by climate change, demographic pressures, urbanization, organized crime, cybersecurity, disinformation, and technological disruption. In short, peacebuilding must move beyond managing the crisis of yesterday and begin preparing humanity for the challenges of tomorrow. Tomorrow. And for that, the peacebuilding architecture of the United Nations, which as I've said we have had the privilege of working with from day one, needs now to move beyond just a UN peacebuilding response. But today's complex challenges require a whole of UN response, and it's why I'm happy that the USG is here, because you cover a wider spectrum. This is why this peacebuilding week matters, because the question before us is not whether the world is changing—it is changing. The question is whether peacebuilding will change with it. For generations, reformers, revolutionaries, and visionaries have asked a simple question: What is to be done? That remains the defining question of our time. What is to be done to ensure that peacebuilding remains relevant? What is to be done to ensure that it remains innovative? What is to be done to ensure that it remains relevant and inclusive? What is to be done to ensure that ordinary people continue to have a stake in shaping their own futures? What is to be done to ensure that technology serves humanity rather than humanity serving technology? And what is to be done to ensure that peace remains a global public good rather than a privilege enjoyed by the few. Excellencies, colleagues, I sometimes wonder what future generations will say about our moment. Will they say that this was the period when humanity surrendered its urgency to power, technology and fear? Or will they say that this was the moment when humanity paused—like we are doing today—reflected, and chose a different path? Will they say that freedom slowly gave way to control? Or will they say that we found the wisdom to harness innovation while protecting dignity, rights, and human freedom? Will they say that peacebuilders became irrelevant? Or will they say that peacebuilders reinvented themselves and helped guide the world through one of the greatest transitions in human history? The proverbial fork in the road is not somewhere beyond the horizon. It is here. We can already see it. One road is illuminated by the bright lights of power, profit, competition, and technological supremacy. The other is illuminated by something less visible but far more enduring: our shared humanity. The first road promises dominance. The second road promises dignity. The first road may appear exciting. The second requires courage. But every generation is eventually asked a question that defines its place in history. Our generation is being asked that question now. Will we build a world that is merely secure, or will we build a world that is secure and free? Will we build a world that is efficient, or will we build a world that is just? Will we build a future for technology, or will we ensure that technology serves the future of humanity? That is why we are here this week—to gather evidence, to challenge assumptions, to imagine new possibilities, to mobilize new partnerships, to tell policymakers, innovators and investors alike that value—the value of peace for humanity is greater. Let me repeat that: the value of peace peace for humanity is greater than the paper valuation of any balance sheet, even if it is a trillion dollars; to affirm that a more secure, more inclusive, more caring and more peaceful world remains possible; and to choose consciously, courageously, the road less travelled. Let those of us who still believe in a better world,— I hope we all do— a more humane world, a more peaceful world, a rules-based and values-driven world, become the voices that inspire others to walk that road with us. Not because it is easy, because it is necessary. Not because success is guaranteed, but because the alternative is unacceptable. Because peace is not naïve. Peace is not weakness. Peace is not an afterthought. Peace is the foundation upon which freedom, justice, prosperity and human dignity are built. And peace, Excellency and colleagues, is not simply the absence of war. Peace is humanity's most ambitious act of hope. And hope, my friends, when organized, mobilized and acted upon, remains the most powerful force in the world. I thank you. It's now my pleasure to hand the floor to the Under-Secretary-General to give her input. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Then thank you for your comments. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, it's a pleasure to address you today during this inaugural Peacebuilding Week. This occasion provides a valuable opportunity to reflect on two decades of United Nations peacebuilding efforts while generating renewed momentum for the work that lies ahead. Throughout this week, your contributions have been central, shaping discussions on prevention, women's inclusion, financing, and the role of artificial intelligence. The networks you represent are among the United Nations' most critical partners in peacebuilding, driving the innovation, inclusion, and impact our work needs. Today, we take stock of the CSO-UN Dialogue Initiative, now entering its fourth year. The presence of all 17 members of the Dialogue's Organizing Core Group reflects both your dedication and the value of this platform. I also thank the Government of Switzerland for its continued support to the Dialogue and to civil society engagement. Nao, Excellencies and colleagues. Since our last meeting in Geneva 6 months ago, the global context has become more challenging. We continue to witness rising geopolitical tensions, protracted conflicts, growing polarization, and shrinking civic space. At the same time, multilateral cooperation is under strain. And resources for peacebuilding and prevention are under pressure. In this context, partnership between civil society and the United Nations is critical. As demands increase and resources diminish, we must work together more effectively. In Geneva, discussions converged on four priorities. First, strengthening civil society as strategic partners and protecting civic space. Second, enhancing system-wide coherence, including through engagement with women and youth-led actors. Third, advancing inclusive and locally-led approaches, including Women, Peace and Security and Youth, Peace and Security. And fourth, improving financing for peacebuilding. A clear message also emerged: the need to move beyond dialogue towards stronger partnerships, joint advocacy, and collective action for impact. Today's meeting reflects our shared commitment to sustained follow-up on these priorities. I hope Peacebuilding Week can serve annually as a moment for reflection, while also feeding the dialogue's outcomes into key processes at UN headquarters, including the Peacebuilding Fund's NEXT Strategy. As we are here primarily to hear from civil society, I will be brief and highlight one good practice and offer two suggestions. First, it is encouraging to see the momentum behind regional CSO-UN dialogues, which translate global priorities into actionable outcomes. Over the past year, 9 regional dialogues have taken place across diverse contexts. Recent meetings in Dakar and in Bangkok brought together civil society, UN colleagues, and partners to deepen regional analysis and generate practical recommendations. This model strengthens the link between field realities and policy, and we welcome these insights and encourage you to share them with colleagues across the United Nations system during your time in New York. Second, I encourage future dialogues to further engage with nationally owned prevention strategies, as discussed this week. These are gaining importance as risks intensify. From Mauritania to Papua New Guinea, promising practices show how civil society networks can support both prioritization and implementation of preventive action. These strategies also provide an entry point to advance key priorities, including women's and youth engagement and financing. Now, in my department, we are supporting prevention approaches that are nationally owned, locally grounded, and internationally supported. Civil society networks play a critical role in sharing good practice and informing global debates. Finally, I wish to reiterate the importance of engagement with the Peacebuilding Commission. The 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review calls for stronger interaction with civil society, including local, women-led, and youth-led organizations. The Commission's monitoring framework offers a useful avenue for the dialogue to inform the intergovernmental deliberations, and I encourage your continued engagement. In today's context, none of us can act alone. Civil society, member states, The United Nations Secretariat must move forward together to strengthen peacebuilding for the challenges ahead, and my department remains fully committed to this partnership. I wish you continued good discussions while you are here in New York and beyond. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Under-Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, representatives of civil society organizations, ladies and gentlemen. Your presence is a reminder that peacebuilding begins long before it reaches conference rooms in Geneva or New York. It starts in communities through the daily efforts of those working to prevent conflict, build trust, and strengthen social cohesion. It is critical that these experiences and realities inform discussions at the policy level, and conversely, that policy deliberations remain anchored in realities on the ground. The CSO-UN dialogue plays an important role in this regard by helping connect international discussions with local experiences. Our collective objective should be to ensure that such engagement becomes a regular and institutionalized feature of our work rather than a periodic exercise. Drawing on their experience and areas of focus from policy to development to humanitarian, human rights, and operational perspectives can help make peacebuilding more coherent and more effective. As a country with a longstanding commitment to dialogue, mediation, and inclusive peacebuilding. Switzerland attaches great importance to strengthening these connections. Mr. Chair, Vasu, thank you very much. Under-Secretary-General, Ambassador Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished colleagues and friends. It's my absolute pleasure and privilege to be here alongside these distinguished opening speakers and my colleagues and friends in the core group of the CSO-UN Dialogue on Peacebuilding. It has been thrilling to be part of the first ever, well overdue UN Peacebuilding Week, and to see how much attention and people conflict prevention and peacebuilding are attracting at this otherwise grim and challenging time that we are living. Håning. Young me could not in my wildest dreams have imagined that I would be back 20 years later alongside you guys talking about this. I think it's important that we stop and consider the significance of the UN leadership and membership coming together at this fragmented and conflict-ridden time and around peacebuilding based on a consensual— consensual adoption of the twin resolution on the peacebuilding architecture review in December last year. It's a recognition of how achieving sustainable peace requires nationally and locally led and owned processes with civil society at the center. And that peacebuilding has greater impact when the UN successfully connects with national and local peacebuilding efforts. Yet civil society has not necessarily been up front and center of this Peacebuilding Week until now. Discussions have largely been centered around UN member states and traditional formats. While I understand why it is particularly important at this time to ensure the UN member states' ownership and therefore commitment to peacebuilding, I do think that it comes at the expense of a certain lost opportunity to really get into the fabric of what peacebuilding is and what is required for peacebuilding to sustain in the current political and financial pressures that we are all under. We need to hear from people on the ground who are the ones who on a daily basis are building peace around the world in both protracted and active conflicts., and in contexts that are at risk of conflicts breaking out. In the large majority of cases, civil society are the last ones to pick up arms and the first ones to build peace. We are on the front line. This is why this inclusion event is so important and why the CSO-UN Dialogue on Peacebuilding is so important. The CSO-UN Dialogue is a prime example of that and a UN leadership who is looking to civil society for a more equal and strategic partnership at a difficult time for multilateralism, for civil society, and for peacebuilding. CMI/Matteo Zara Peace Foundation is a proud founding member of the Core Group and a former co-chair of the CSO-UN Dialogue with the UN last year. This allows for mutual learning and also trust building, and thus more strategic, forward-looking discussions on how to better and more effectively build peace. Thank you. Thank you, Joubeka. And yes, Graeme's sufficient. Excellencies, colleagues, I'm going to try and take only a little time I think we've heard a— I feel a little bit like the cheese in the sandwich. All the deep analytical reflection on the current context has happened, and then after this there will be the reflective exercise of looking at what we've been doing and how and asking all the tough questions about what's worked, what happened, what were the challenges, what were the achievements. And in between, I'm just going to do this little sliver of history, which mostly reflects, I think, some of the innovative practice that we sometimes take for granted in how this UN CSO dialogue has evolved. And some of what I think you described at the beginning, Ibek, is true, that I think there was quite a lot of risk, that we didn't know what this was going to be like, and that this is is a process that has been shaped by the protagonists in it. It has been driven by an exercise that has involved leaps of faith, quite a lot of disciplined, contested, honest discussion, and at the base of all of it, eventually, the construction of a really safe space in which there's a high degree of trust both between the civil society organizations in the core group and beyond in this exercise, which is not to suggest it's perfect, and between the CSOs and the CSO core group and the UN. So the first UN dialogue took place in 2023. The next one will take place at the end of 2026. Over 20 years after the establishment of the peacebuilding architecture. I think in some ways— well, over the last two days, over the last week in the course of this historic first inaugural peacebuilding week in New York, largely thanks to the generous support of Switzerland in bringing the core group members to New York to participate in this, for which we're very grateful, and an incredible hard work of Rebecca and her very small, very overworked team. We've had the luxury of a day and a half's worth of reflection, a much-needed process on the dialogues going back to '23, '24, and last year in Geneva in '25. I think that the— it's easy considering this is the— this will be the fourth year in which the dialogue takes place to see it as almost institutionalized, but actually the drive and the demand of civil society organizations throughout this process has been for exactly that and a recognition that that is not yet a complete process. That it is about recognizing the importance of institutionalizing in some ways the role of civil society actors in the deliberations of the multilateral system. This is still a work in progress. It's not predetermined. It wasn't predetermined that this would take root, and we have to keep pushing on these buttons in order to make this happen. At origin, I think the first dialogue driven by a UN recognizing that as we approached the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review, there needed to be a more organized, more predictable, less ad hoc engagement with the peacebuilding field and access to the innovation, perspectives, and practice of CSOs, of organized peacebuilders on the ground, both the practice, the policy perspectives, and the analytical research and understanding of this field rooted in the practice of peacebuilding on the ground. So the first dialogue in December 2023 was a precursor to the Peacebuilding Architecture Review of '25., and it was a process that was quite fraught with risk. It involved 50, roughly 50 civil society organizations. There had been the selection of core group members of the dialogue, civil society core group members, who were largely, not exclusively, regionally based networks, and it was essentially up to those networks in the first iteration of this to handpick and select the civil society organizations that would come to New York for that first dialogue. I think there was a strong sense that this would be an opportunity from the UN side to brief civil societies, to make sure that civil society organizations were well informed. I think there was a sense that this would become a vehicle for consultative process leading into the PBAR, with some risk that this could be about quite an extractive exchange. The terms of reference worked out together of the dialogue was about enabling the policy contribution of CSOs and enabling the UN to more systematically engage with them.. And that, in a sense, was quite a bland and uncomplicated mandate, but it came in that first dialogue with some real risks. The risk was that this would be one-way traffic, that civil society organizations would step into the space and be briefed, that they would share their views, and that this would be absorbed. But in some ways, and I have to say, as the first co-chair of the process, I think we came into this quite wary of that, quite wary that this could be a way of oversimplifying or rubber stamping consultations with civil society. And I think it was largely through the reciprocal commitments But really civil society organizations' determination in that first process that the space was shaped, that actually this was described not as a consultation process but as a dialogue, that this wasn't about one party briefing the other but that it was about reciprocal learning, it was about honest, reflective, engagement with innovative practice. I don't think that could be taken for granted. In the wake of that, I think there was also— and this is where the trust was really built— a real recognition that we had to together challenge the way we traditionally did things, the different cultural spaces that the UN and civil society organizations often operate— operated under. It required the negotiation and co-creation of agendas, which was not the same as inviting people into a space in which the agenda had already been set. It required being quite brave about challenging existing formats, traditional formats for the way in which these conversations happened. The protocols of diplomacy which often provided real opportunities for exclusion rather than inclusion, the privileging of voices through the order of who spoke when, the need to broaden both the participants on the UN side and the CSO side of who was in that process. And there was a real exercise— I remember this— in the development of the second CSO-UN Dialogue Agenda, a real conversation about how we needed to take every single panel and reorder and juggle with the way in which speakers were organized so that we made sure that no one was second in line all the time, that there was a real balancing act in those processes, and that took quite a lot of courage. It took quite a lot of innovation. It really was a vital process in building trust and the trustworthiness of this forum, its openness to being reshaped through this collaborative endeavor and a recognition that we had to try and do things differently. So if we were slightly on guard in 2023, worried that this would be a once-a-year talkshop, or that it could become an annual jamboree in which an extractive exercise took place once a year. Actually, there was a real collaboration, a real collaboration ensuring that that was not the case and that in 2024 the agenda was a co-designed one, it was co-created, it had a different set of criteria for participation, and that included our ability together and I emphasize together, to rethink how we invited civil society organizations into that space. 2024 was really important because instead of the CSOs who were part of the core group selecting who would be in the room, we actually established a set of criteria, a quite laborious and time-demanding process of applications, and we invited organizations based on a set of criteria, thematic focuses, a set of priorities to apply to come, and that completely changed the composition of who was in the room and how that was determined. And that also took quite a lot of innovation and courage. There was a commitment to the rotation of the chairs of the core group. There was a commitment, at least in principle, to rotation of the members of the core group— sorry, the co-chair of the dialogue and the members of the core group. And that was very important because it wasn't just about changing the way the UN did things, it was also about recognizing the importance of eliminating the potential for small politics, competitive discourse within the civil society organizations. And there was a real commitment to thinking about this as an evolving process in which we had to establish continuity between the agendas, the outcome documents, some kind of accountability from one year to the next. This was a real change and a real shift in how this process evolved. It scaled up civil society involvement, but it also was a big push for scaling up and diversifying the number of— the UN agencies engaging with the dialogue, and a real push in '24 to sort of expand this to a conversation which also invited in and included member states. So at the same time, I think it was very determined to preserve the opportunity to listen to initiative from the field and to ensure that this conversation was one which really accessed civil society voice, not just as policy advice, as I say, but as innovative peacebuilding practice to access the research and analysis of civil society and new voices through that process. 2025 took the dialogue from New York to Geneva, and I think this is really important. This wasn't just about moving from one hub to another.. It wasn't just about moving the geography of this. It was, at least in part, about a recognition of the fact that we needed to also talk to different UN agencies and entities, that peace was not going to be forged just in New York and just within the structures of the peacebuilding architecture in New York, but that there was the opportunity to actually engage humanitarian, human rights, development, and other UN agencies and entities in a spirit of recognizing that peacebuilding was a cross-cutting goal across the UN system. This was associated also with the push for a lot of civil society organizations who were saying, "Actually, the place we meet the UN is not in New York, and it's not always through the architecture of the peacebuilding structures that are based in New York." This means moving beyond one-off consultations and towards more structured and institutionalized practices and participation where civil societies youth can engage consistently through negotiation, implementation, and follow-up. Last year, myCP and other partners conducted consultations which examined existing gaps in practices, and these exchanges point to 5 priority areas for consideration. One, institutionalizing youth participation across peace processes through formal and sustainable advisory, negotiation, and implementation monitoring mechanisms. Second is ensuring meaningful rather symbolic inclusion, such as youth contributions informing agenda setting, decision making, and follow-up across peace channels, such as the UN Civil Society Dialogue. Third, integrating displacement and mobility into peacebuilding and mediation, recognizing the agency, expertise, and lived experience of displaced youth as relevant to conflict prevention, social cohesion. Fourth, strengthening intergenerational and cross-sectional dialogue amongst mediators, policymakers, and youth peacebuilders. And lastly, fifth, establishing follow-up mechanism including the CSO dialogues that translate youth engagement into sustainable institutional commitments at local and international levels. Ultimately, strengthening the civil society organization youth engage— UN engagement is not simply about creating more opportunities to speak, it's to ensure that decisions are being generally reflected into reality expertise, and solutions of communities most impacted so that peacebuilding becomes more sustainable, effective, and inclusive. Thank you.

That this is about the local lived experience, our job to create the platforms, amplify it, not romanticize it, not isolate and insulate it, because our translocal horizontal learning is not just a learning between the UN and CSOs, it's a learning within the civil society sector, within the peacebuilding practitioner space. But that's really changing the conversation about localization as an amplification up, as a different power, assertion of power in that space. It's actually about how policy is shaped from below. I think there was really powerful conversation here about trust, and I— shame, Hannah's going to go mad from this— I always talk about how we need to stop talking about trust, because that often imposes the onus on those who we want to trust the system rather than trustworthiness, which is that the system has to prove itself to those people. There is a conversation here which is, I think, embracing this conversation about trust and trustworthiness at the heart of what we're doing, at trying to find a different and a common institutional culture across the CSOs and the UN from very different places that is necessary and driven by the transactional world and politics that we're engaging with and the greater need now than ever before to find a common ground, to defend it, and to do it with real sincerity because the enemy is not in the room, it's out there in terms of where global politics is going. I think there was a really fascinating set of issues that came out about One of the consequences of this process, which is perhaps an unintended consequence but one which has been grasped, and that is that this has become a vehicle for building the regional networks, for building the translocal connections, and we've seen examples of where that's happening. And our, our interest in actually moving this conversation into a more decentralized space has actually played a really important support catalytic role in potentially sort of sustaining the energy, if not the resources, to build those kinds of local or more regional conversations. I think there's a really important conversation which is self-reflective and self-critical that's in the room from the civil society actors. It's expressed as always and unsurprisingly through the youth lens, which is stop tokenizing participation. We recognize the challenge of expanding our own access and representation, whether it's disability groups or whether it's greater participation of women or it's a different set of indigenous actors, et cetera, et cetera. But I think there's a real recognition of the fact that one of the challenges of the CSO, the institutionalization of the CSO role, is always going to be who do you represent and on what basis do you represent people. And we have to embrace that and we have to do it as a demonstration effect by constantly expanding our own commitment to inclusion and diversifying that. And I think that's come out here in really interesting ways from different perspectives. I think there's a real valuation here of innovation, but at the same time there's a reality check that I've heard from a number of the inputs, which is that there is always a really grave danger, however much we talk about dialogue as co-creation and co-invention, and flat rather than hierarchical, there is still nonetheless a real danger that if we don't recognize what dialogue looks like and where it fails when the demand is protection, there is often a sense that dialogue can be seen as different to action. And we have to recognize the demands for protection, the shutting down of civic space, that the luxury of our conversation here is not replicated in the spaces in which many of the people here come from. And so it's not a simple exercise of let's take this from the global to the local or localize it. It's actually a recognition of the fact that the constraints at the local level and the civic space constraints and the lack of protection issues and the transactional nature of politics and the reclamation of ugly power and the securitization of the peacebuilding agenda actually are barriers that we have to navigate and overcome. So I'm going to leave it at that. I do think there were some important points made. I love the fact that there are member states represented in the room that are as inspired by this as we are. So I share your— the collective appreciation here of what this voice looks like. And our onerous, and particularly Accord's onerous obligation with the PBPSO to take this forward. Why I raise that and why I raise the fact that you— a number of young people here— because you're a new generation entering a new era. We are a generation that exits an era that we thought we were creating this really powerful world. It's a much more difficult time. When the peace-building architecture was founded in 2005, The population of the world was about 6.5 billion people. We're about 8.3 billion today. That's 2 billion more people in the world. Much more complex, uh, transnational organized criminal syndicates, insurgencies that are not ideologically driven, they're transactionally driven. These are dangerous times. Urbanization, that is a reality that we never saw 40 years ago or so, but the rate at urbanization is taking place and the complexities around social cohesion, the hatred around the world, the democratic backsliding, you as a generation are entering a very dangerous world. It's not a cliché to say that you got to take it very seriously. This is about your future. As you're the generation in a decade from now will be sitting in the UN as decision makers. So, I'm encouraged to see you here. Stay the course. It will be difficult. It will take courage. And I encourage you to have the courage to shape your own future. So thank you very much. I can't, it's so hard to follow that. No, come on, you say a few words and then I'll do what I did previously. And I'm like 3 days into this job. So please. Yeah, yeah, that's great. A lifetime in the UN. In fact, you know, when I was working, I started in CSO, International NGO, in Asia, Indonesia. And then at some point, I was offered a job in the UN. And my impression of the UN was not good, right? I really felt that the UN was just a lot of talk, and I didn't see a lot of action in changing things on the ground. And I asked my boss, who was an incredible person, and he was very wise, and he said, think of the power behind that flag. And what you can do in the organization. So I jumped over and became that other, and I saw some incredible things, especially when I joined in this area where I was working initially in the area of HIV/AIDS. And at that time, civil society— we had enough money and enough collaboration across the UN system that we were able to partner with civil society with the theme of "Nothing for us without us." And that came from, you know, sex workers in Asia-Pacific who said, "We're tired of you telling us what to do, how to live our lives, what to do with our bodies. We want to have that discussion directly with member states." And we were able at that time to bring transgender people, sex workers, gay men, the whole gamut of people affected by that epidemic, straight to member states where they could talk about issues and what needed to change. It was an incredible time because, you know, I never imagined the power of the UN in bringing people who could never have a voice or never express their voice to people in power. And that's the best of the UN, that we can do that. And I feel we've backslided— is that a word? Backslipped. We've gone back. And when I look around now, and I'm most recently a resident coordinator, and I know the limitations of partnership at country level. And I know the frustration. And we talk about trustworthiness. How do we build that trust? Clearly, there are many things that we need to do on our side to improve. And in this area of peacebuilding, more important than ever that we partner with CSOs. What I saw on the ground in Papua New Guinea, where I was Resident Coordinator, was the best examples of peacebuilding were very grassroots. So when I see women on the ground, one woman from the Catholic Church, a nun that was going out and rescuing women who were being tortured because they were accused of sorcery-based violence in a conflict setting and willing to take that risk. And also how the communities work together to set up support systems and safe houses and help people move to other places and safe places. So there are so many good examples of peacebuilding building where women leaders in the community were coming together and saying, 'Stop this fighting. We have to stop. The men must stop this fighting.' Very effective ways of advocating at community level. So the best practices are on the ground. And how do you bring that up to country level and to regional level? The only way is with partnerships with CSOs. So I firmly believe that this regional platform, the global platform, the regional dialogues is a very important first step, but we need to take it to country level now. So some practical ideas I'd just like to raise today, because as we transition to UN80, we will have a smaller footprint at country level. UN agencies will move away from that project mentality, project modality, and start to focus more on advocacy, policy advocacy, technical advice, which opens up a space for civil society to do more on implementation in partnership with the UN, in partnership with government or others. So I think now is the time to figure out a different way of working where civil society plays a greater role. So one is in this advisory capacity. There are many entry points. I know a lot of you are frustrated, how do you get into the RC office? There are partnership officers, there are peace and development advisors. Some of the best people are your human rights advisors. They're the, the most outward-facing in many places, so utilize those channels. Of course, agencies like UNDP, UNFPA, UN Women, they're also more effectively inclined towards civil society. That's also an entry point, but there has to be, in countries with a prevention strategy, civil society advisory around that strategy. In countries developing the strategy, they need to be there at the table when the strategy is developed. Also in monitoring, you know, monitoring, holding governments accountable and line ministries accountable to implement that strategy. It's your RC and the team that can place or help to facilitate that role in the advisory capacity. And the second is implementation partners. And that's the harder one because we tend to treat CSOs as contractors at best. You know, sometimes we just go around and ask your advice and go away and never come back. Or we ask you to participate in an evaluation and never come back. So you probably feel like you're being mined constantly and not given a role that you deserve, that you must play as an equal partner. So how to move beyond that? Clearly, funding modalities is also a challenge. I mean, you have to have very thick skin as a CSO, a great resilience to navigate our financial rules and procedures. We're not doing it because of lack of trust. It's our audit systems require the same procedure for a $30 million project as it does for a $300 million workshop— a $300 workshop. The systems tie our hands, so we have to find more flexible funding modalities. As we move to pooled funding setups at country level, can we have a CSO window that's a bit more flexible? And so that's very important that we find a way at country level. We have to move, and what we'd like to do is move— am I talking too long? Moving beyond where we've come so far, which is incredible, to really practical ways of working in these two areas at country level. So with that, I just want to deliver a few lines from my very important remarks, which is to thank all of the partners involved that have supported these dialogues up to date, including Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, Australia, and Germany. In this era of declining ODA and declining support for civil society organizations, the fact that you have stood behind this effort is incredibly appreciated. Also great to see Canada here and in putting very important— bringing people. Also thanking all of you who have been here throughout and continue to have faith in the UN and how you can partner with us. Don't give up. We have to find a way, and I think country level is a way to start to make it work. So with that, all I do is say from PBPSO, that we will stay on this course with you and we're going to get to that next level of implementation in the year ahead. So hold us accountable for that. And thank you all. And it was a pleasure being here today and listening to you.
